summary:
Yaroslavl Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned outright, changes of gender marker on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. A transgender visitor therefore cannot obtain or amend documents reflecting their gender while in the oblast, and has no lawful route to gender-affirming care in the country.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' statute is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with a repeated offence escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years under Article 282.2. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and official national government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers.

Enforcement operates at volume. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols, roughly 98 of them administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty across 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. It assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection, and it affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

Yaroslavl Oblast applies this national framework without a local carve-out. The oblast's Sirotkin criminal case is the only recorded deviation from the national enforcement baseline, making it the single region-specific data point in this dossier rather than a description of local conditions.
tangentialFactors:
The United States State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers; the UK Home Office note sets the standard for UK asylum claims and affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, form a particular social group under the refugee convention. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia.

Enforcement volume is rising alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two preceding years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Moscow Times reporting of 23 June 2025 described arrests, club raids and extremism charges as the defining features of LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman who called herself a second-class citizen after the designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. BBC Russian reporting of 27 July 2024 followed a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Residents of Yaroslavl Oblast face the same document and healthcare prohibitions as visitors, but for them the consequences are structural rather than temporary: a gender marker cannot be amended on a Russian passport or any other official document, and no lawful route to gender-affirming care exists within the country at all.

Administrative liability under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols and criminal liability under Article 282.2 for participation in or organisation of the designated movement apply to residents with the penalties stated above. Human Rights Watch counted 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases and at least 20 people facing criminal charges between January 2024 and June 2025 nationally.

The UK Home Office assessment that openly LGBT+ people are likely to experience treatment amounting to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them, governs UK asylum determinations and rests on a record of at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

The Sirotkin criminal case in Yaroslavl Oblast is the only deviation from the national enforcement record identified for the region.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory names the Sirotkin criminal case in Yaroslavl Oblast as the region's only deviation from the national framework but does not supply its charges, procedural stage, date, or outcome. That case remains unresolved as evidence and is not characterised here beyond its existence.

No sourcing in the inventory establishes enforcement activity specific to Yaroslavl Oblast: the count of propaganda-law or extremism cases brought in the oblast, local police or prosecutor practice, and any oblast-level directives are not sourced and remain unverified.

The availability of trans-specific care providers, the treatment of gender markers in practice at local registry offices, and the physical safety environment for transgender visitors in the oblast's cities are not covered by the supplied sources.

Whether federal 'propaganda' enforcement has been applied to oblast-level media, libraries, or public events in Yaroslavl Oblast is not sourced in this inventory.
